BASILICA CHYMICA. a

[Large decorative initial S] The CURES of all diseases (as I shall also use here, most appropriately, the significant words of P. Severinus b) are twofold.
UNIVERSAL, which is the removal of the Roots or morbid impurities, whether from birth or hereditarily from the seed of parents c, or later from the use and fault of foods, or from the injury of external Impressions implanted in the Human Anatomy: it is perfected by a Natural Balsam of Remedies agreeable to Human Nature d, dissolving, consuming, and dissipating the seminal Tinctures of Impurities: and indeed strengthening, consolidating, and preserving the Innate Balsam (for as long as, according to Paracelsus, the radical moisture remains in its quantity, no disease is felt.)
[Marginal note: There is one common Mumia of all humans, therefore the Spirit of life and one Medicine can exist, because disease in man is nothing other than an affection by which the function of the Mumia or Spirit of life in man is impeded.]
And because here pluralities of indications, particularities, [and] orders have no place, it is resolved by one and the same Remedy. Therefore Lullius says not without reason that this one supreme and universal medicine, to which all particular medicines are reduced, can be administered to the Human body without knowledge of the infirmity, because wise Nature, through its instinct, gave it the Virtues of curing all natural infirmities and of rectifying itself. The four highest kinds of diseases e exalted f

**CHYMICA. 7**
nothing but the most select medicines.
It seems to be of Germanic origin, as if *Baltsamen*.

**b** For in the preface, the same Severinus the Dane used words from chapter 14 of the Idea of Medical Philosophy. Many think that Peter Severinus is not the author of the Idea, but that Pratensis, whose poem is annexed at the end, which the comparison of the poem and the whole writing seems to indicate.

**c** Seed must be distinguished from sperma. Sperma is that whole body which is seen by the eyes, but seed is a part in any grain or sperma.

**d** Remedies ought to be similar to balsam; this is the highest axiom of physicians introduced by the Dictator Hippocrates into sound Therapeutics in book 2, On Flatulence, and Aphorism 22. Opposites are remedies for opposites. To this seems opposed the dictum of the Hermetics: Likes are cured by likes. But there is no appearance of contradiction, but both must be rightly understood: Remedies, namely, ought to be similar to nature, or to balsam and native heat, which they ought to help in conquering disease, but they ought to be contrary to the disease itself.

I.

UNIVERSAL DIGESTIVE
or Maturative. [crescent moon symbol with a dot]

IN diseases which consist of mobile b superficial impurities, which have not struck fixed c roots, nor are destined d for difficult coagulations – which is detected from the characteristic signs e of pains and the inconstant and swollen effervescences of symptoms, such as very many f fevers, Catarrhs, Coughs, Hoarseness, and similar affections – in these, there is no need for a Digestive; they are safely and quickly removed by the aid of Purgatives and Cleansers. But febrile g and inflammatory impurities, which have more difficult Tinctures, because they admit fixed resolutions and coagulations of Vapors: difficult to resolve (such are perpetually found in suspected h parts and corresponding minerals,) are most safely and conveniently cured by the Concoction of Hippocrates, or the Mitigation of Paracelsus, or the Epicrasis of Galen (namely, equivalent curative indications); for they do not yield to the crude faculties of common Purgative medicines, which act with corporeal and crude spirits, which Spirits

VITRIOLATED TARTAR. a

[marginal note: C]

♃. Take. b Of the purest Tartar Salt, several times
according to the Chymical art dissolved, filtered &
coagulated with agrimony water, c for example,
four ounces, resolve in a chamber upon marble,
or by means of a sleeve into oil. Having obtained this
pure oil, take of most excellently rectified oil of Vitriol d
two ounces, and instill that drop by drop e upon the Tartar
oil in a capacious glass: then a most white coagulum will be made,
the supernatant humidity should be drawn off by gentle
heat to the dryness of the Salt, thus is obtained
white fixed Vitriolated Tartar. f.

**CHEMISTRY. 17**

**Observations.**

[Marginal note:]
If too small a quantity of oil of Vitriol is poured in, it causes at least vomiting.

I. Let moderation be observed in pouring in the *oil of Vitriol*, lest the taste of the repercussed Salt be too acidic, but rather nauseating: for if too much of the *oil of Vitriol* is poured in, then it does not purge, otherwise it operates through four excretory channels: vomiting, g stool (if h mixed with purgatives), likewise through urine and sweat.

II. If it can be done through a funnel i with a very narrow opening, so that by a certain artifice drops of *oil of Vitriol* may drip gradually and successively into the *oil of Tartar*, it will be more advisable, for thus the good spirits, which rise as vapor and vanish from the mutual effervescence of the sudden mixture, will be retained.

[Handwritten marginal note:]
Sennertus denies [this].

III. The *glass* heats up excessively from the conjunction of those two Fires. K In this mutual effervescence, let the generation of Epilepsy be observed, when, namely, the Spirit of Life in the Microcosm, excited by Heterogeneous [elements], boils up in a similar manner l.

IV. Whoever wishes to add one part of Salt or liquor of Corals to two m parts of *oil of Tartar*, before pouring in the *oil of Vitriol* drop by drop, let it be entirely up to him.

A Digestive can be prepared from that *Vitriolated Tartar*, which, when necessity demands n, must be administered before purgative medicines, in this manner.

The rawest white tartar is coarsely pounded, washed and rinsed with simple clear water until all impurities are removed, and the powder is white, without dregs. Afterwards, spring water is added to a height of one palm above, and it is boiled in a larger earthen pot until a supernatant pellicle appears. Then, with the pot removed from the fire and exposed in a cooler place, the gradually growing crystals are finally removed and collected, along with the small stones adhering to the sides of the vessel beneath the water. Dry and reduce to powder (this cream does a great deal for those who have difficulty purging their bowels). Repeat this boiling and collection of the pellicle and crystals often, namely, until a sufficient quantity is obtained.

It is a supreme deobstruent in hypochondriac melancholy, both for the bowels and for tartar lodging in the spleen and mesenteric veins. The dose should be repeated often. In other respects, it is equal in virtues to Vitriolated Tartar.

PREPARATION OF THE SAFFRON OF METALS.

Recipe. Of pure, well-purified niter 1 or 2 pounds, of antimony the same amount. Let the niter melt in a pan with a very slow fire, yet without any violent ignition of the vessel. Remove the vessel from the fire and add the antimony, well and finely pulverized. If they allow themselves to be mixed together without inflammation and detonation, that is good. But if not, desist for a while until the niter, having obtained sufficient cooling, can completely endure and retain the antimony powder, gradually at first, but afterwards by mixing it in a mass. Indeed, let all things be continually stirred with an iron spatula. When all things have been thoroughly mixed together, ignite the whole with live charcoal, or rather with a red-hot iron. When they have detonated, the Saffron of Metals is prepared. Then indeed, the Antimony elaborated in this way is left not unlike saffron.
USE OF THE SAFFRON OF METALS.
The general use and dose is 6 or 12 grains. Let them be macerated, and in urgent necessity let them boil in water, or wine, or beer, or mead, or any other liquid whatsoever, provided that they themselves

However, equivalent to the same water is a simple infusion of glass of Antimony by itself, without any addition whatsoever, either of flux (that is, borax) or of any other prepared thing, prepared in Rhenish white wine. Pulverized glass, for example, ℥ j. or ℥ ij., are infused in ℔. iij. or iiij. of wine; and the glass vessel being well and firmly covered, they are exposed to the sun for some time, until indeed the liquid takes on a citrine color; afterwards it is filtered, and in turn, it is kept in a well-closed glass vessel. Its use, from ʒ j. to ʒ iij. or to ʒ v. at most, in appropriate distilled water, is given to induce vomiting, with great benefit, especially in those diseases which can and will not be cured otherwise than by vomiting: such as are all coughs, pleurisies, anginas, anorexias, eructations, and countless others residing in the first region of the belly. CAUTIONS IN THE ADMINISTRATION
_OF WATER, AND OTHER THINGS, MOST_
_NECESSARY TO KNOW._

1. Those are to be purged by vomiting: Who easily

38 **BASILICA**

...vomit, have a strong stomach, are broad-chested, with a firm head, accustomed to vomiting, and for whom the morbid matter is carried upwards.

	2. Picrocholic individuals, and those who are called *pterygodes* by physicians, who are weak in strength and vomit with difficulty; likewise, those who are subject to headache, hemorrhage, suffusion of the eyes, diseases of the lungs, lipothymia, and suffocation of the uterus, are not rashly to be provoked to vomit, as pseudo-chemists and empirics are wont to do, and who often boldly and wickedly play with another's skin.

	3. He who is about to administer the blessed water and other emetics should accurately consider the circumstances: lest anything be too much or too little; that it be done opportunely; what should be done beforehand, what afterwards.

	4. The most opportune time for administering emetics is the waxing Moon. For then
[A horizontal line is drawn across the page]
the luxuriant and swollen humors are safely and easily expelled by vomiting.

	5. He who is about to vomit should keep himself warm, and cherish his vital parts with warm cloths: lest from cooling, griping pains arise, as often happens.

	6. Beer should not be administered immediately after the emetic has been taken, but only after the patient has vomited two or three times. For otherwise it blunts the force of the emetic, it does not promote it.

11. One should not oversleep after emetics: especially for bilious constitutions: lest bile be carried into the brain through sleep. When, however, the patient seems to have vomited enough, sleep can be granted.

III.
RESOLVENT CATHARTIC,
cleansing, abluent.

It is potent with the virtues of Scammony and Colocynth [a].

Observations.

1. Every laxative should consist of three energies, according to Paracelsus: that it may relax Nature (the body) tired from evacuation, strengthen the debilitated, and mitigate [b].
2. Purgations which bring about symptoms that are evidence of still remaining poisonous properties [c], and a depression of strength, are perpetually to be avoided.
3. In the true method of purging (in which we do not estimate the power and excellence of the faculties by the number or quantity of evacuations, but where we perceive the roots of diseases and impurities removed by the remission of symptoms and the restoration of strength), we then judge that the remedies have completed their duty, whether they remove impurities by complete [d] consumption or by sensible excretion, whether they move urines, or pains, or evacuations.
4. Cathartics operate not by the force of quality [e], that is, by reason of heat, cold, humidity, or dryness, but by a hidden property and form.

[Handwritten 'C' in the right margin next to the title]

--- Page 50 ---
**42 BASILICA**
and specific form, namely, by the property of the whole substance, which, by the impulse of heat and an inciting celestial force, expels a humor familiar and akin to itself for excretion.

5. In chronic, f critical, and long-lasting diseases, not Purgations, but Arcana g should be used, for they are not cured without Spagyric processes h.

6. If Purgations are instituted in chronic diseases, they ought to be done slowly, gradually, and over time.

7. Although Plato in Timaeus i prescribes that strong and violent medicines should not be used rashly, nor the body moved inconsiderately, and long before him Hippocrates, who refused to treat his friend and intimate Democritus with Hellebore and similar things, affirming that there is no purgative medicine that does not plunder some part of the strength and substance of our body; and for this reason Avicenna rightly says that even if Medicines K are not poisonous, to drink them l is laborious for Nature: nevertheless, the fixed roots of diseases require Antimonial, Vitriolated, and Mercurial Purgations, from which m we could deservedly abstain, had not a better and innocent n way of preparing them become known, and had not the Intemperance, the nurse of the physicians of this age, despising the frugality of our ancestors, driven us, even unwilling, to their use.

However, it is asked 1. concerning the subject of the purgative faculty, where does it reside? Not in quality alone, [Marginal note: The subject of the purgative faculty, where does it reside?] because that [quality] moves the faculty, and [it is also found] in separated elements: Thus the elements of wine are, burning fire, or igneous air, phlegmatic water, and the earthy portion, namely, of Tartar salt; the whole wine, consisting of these joined together, by the property of its temperament moderately heats, namely, to become fiery, not to inflame: But in the separated spirit or air there is a certain fire in actuality, no temperament there, but a pure, as it were, quality, such as is sought in fire. Therefore this faculty is much less in temperament. Temperament is of things joined and many contraries. It will therefore be in some hypostatic principle, either Salt, Sulfur, or Mercury: But rather in Mercurial salt, than in others, which appears in the extracts of purgatives by spirit of vinegar. Those indeed do not purge equally, as other extracts, wherefore, for example, spirit of vinegar extracts Sulfur, meanwhile the salt remains.

**Observations.**

1.  The sign of a true precipitate is if it is strongly ground with gold q, and the gold is not whitened by it, as usually happens from contact with Mercury.
2.  It is not necessary that it be entirely fixed, r, for by that reason it would lose its purging power.
3.  There is no precipitate that cannot be reduced, s; if it were completely fixed, it could not operate in the human body, t, for by reason of its crudity u it performs its operations.

BEST PURIFICATION OF MERCURY.

♁. Of crude mercury, a sufficient quantity, pour into a whole, rather oblong, not shortened cucurbit, the best spirit of wine to a height of two fingers above it: Then shake for a while, moving it vigorously up and down in your hands, and carefully stopping the upper opening of the cucurbit with your thumb while shaking. You will see all the mercurial blackness separate into the spirit of wine and on the sides of the vessel. Decant the spirit of wine infected with blackness, and pour fresh spirit over it, and likewise, by shaking repeatedly, separate the remaining blackness. Perform this operation until all the blackness has been removed, which in some mercuries contaminated with much dregs, almost a fourth part of their weight equals; Evaporate the spirit of wine by means of a Balneum (water bath), leaving the blackness at the bottom. Reserve that spirit of wine for the same operations, or even for others. By this purification, the mercury shows a most brilliant and supremely celestial color, an excellent test of its purity. EXCELLENT PRECIPITATION OF MERCURY.

First, let aqua fortis be made from 2 pounds of niter, 1 pound of vitriol, 6 ounces of uncalcined alum, 1 ounce of common salt. Mix, distill, and let the water be made in the usual way, as Tyrocinium teaches, book 3, chapter 2. ♃.
Of purified mercury, as much as you wish, dissolve with water, as much as you wish to dissolve (NB. Mercury must be dissolved, namely, as much as can be dissolved by the water, otherwise precipitation does not readily occur). To the mercury thus dissolved, pour on 2 or 3 ounces of cold spring water, and leave for some time in a quiet place, away from fire, for several hours, so that the mercury may precipitate to the bottom of its own accord. **I. GRAY MERCURY, solely purgative.**

1. Take common yellow or white precipitated Mercury; let it be washed often with rose water, and dried: afterwards let it be imbibed with the best spirit of wine, and let equal parts of Camphor dissolved in spirit of wine be added and combined, and in turn, let the spirit of wine be evaporated from it to dryness with a gentle heat, and the Mercury will become gray. The dose of this, from 3 to 6 grains, mixed with extract of Theriac, administered 6 hours before the paroxysm, wonderfully expels all fevers by operating solely through evacuation. It is also a precious Antidote in plague and other epidemic diseases, but especially in the English sweat.

Libavius, in the later volume of badly compiled chemical arcana, denies that this coralline arcanum, attributed to our author Paracelsus, is his, but affirms Crollius or Huser to be the inventor, because it would not be found thus in Paracelsus's works, and he (Paracelsus) himself makes mention of another coralline in book 3, chapter 25, "On Restoring Ill-Cured Patients." Both arguments for this assertion are invalid. Although it does not exist in Paracelsus's published writings and works, nor does it agree with the description of the Coralline which Paracelsus placed in the aforementioned book 3, "On Restoring Ill-Cured Patients," nevertheless, a treatise shows Paracelsus himself to be the author—a treatise which he himself wished to designate as a key and guide to his books, written to a certain friend, but hitherto published by no one, lying hidden among a few, especially Huser, who edited Paracelsus's writings, but recently published in part by Rhenanus in the booklet "The Sun Emerging from the Well." Indeed, at the beginning and end of the same description, he refers the reader to his surgery, where, indeed, treating of the coralline arcanum, he delivered its more abundant virtues, but nowhere does a trace of it appear, except that he treated of the corallate in the previously cited place, with little or nothing corresponding to this description. If therefore Libavius had seen Paracelsus's key, or at least E 3 Ge-

**METHOD OF PRECIPITATING**
**Mercury by itself.**

Let there be made in glass-making workshops compressed and wide phials, scarcely one cubit high inside, and with a very narrow opening hardly admitting a needle. Into the wide bottom let crude mercury, well and thoroughly purified, be introduced, so that it finally covers the bottom, and at least some part of the glass remains empty from the top. Therefore, place it very precisely in sand for equilibrium, so that nowhere the quantity of mercury is higher or lower due to a perhaps uneven position. And heat it first with a slow, then with a stronger fire, until it spontaneously turns into a very red powder, like cinnabar. This powder should be carefully washed with cordial waters or spirit of wine. Let it be administered from 4 to 6 grains. It strongly promotes sweats, and, administered seven or six times, it completely eradicates and eliminates venereal disease, if other things necessary for this cure are also at hand. Moreover, it completely removes all fevers, both continuous and intermittent.

SWEET MERCURY,
Quercetanus's All-Humor Purge.

Sweet Mercury, the "Mitigated Dragon," as it is called by the author of Beguinus's *Tyrocinium Chymicum* (Chemical Novitiate), book 2, chapter 18, is made from sublimated mercury and crude mercury joined in certain weights, and sublimated anew. In this way, the corrosive spirits in the sublimate are indeed removed by a homogeneous artifice, that is, they are "mortified" by quicksilver, and the whole compound is thereby *apoion* (tasteless), that is, it is made without any acrid taste, but tending towards sweetness. Concerning this, read Quercetanus in *Tetras gravissimorum affectuum capitis* (Tetrad of the Most Serious Affections of the Head). The *Tyrocinium* in the cited place adds Colcothar in its preparation, that is, vitriol calcined to redness, but with no necessity. For by themselves, without the addition of any other foreign substance, they easily combine through sublimation.

The method is therefore as follows. ℞. Of pure and sincere sublimated mercury, as I taught in the notes to the said chapter of the *Tyrocinium* edited by Gluckrad, ℥ viij. Of well-purified mercury, ℥ vj. Grinding them together, part by part, mix in a stone mortar, until the quicksilver has been absorbed into the sublimate; then sublimate from a flask, filled only halfway, in

     WHITE FLOWERS OF ANTIMONY.

     For making the white ones, there is an easy method
by the author and the Tyrocinium in the cited place. But they are produced more successfully
if an earthenware cucurbit, made from good ma-

material and lined, is tubulated near the bottom, and to it, after being firmly placed in the furnace, blind alembics receiving each other should be adapted, perforated in that part where they mutually receive each other; their number should be six or more. At the top, a glass beaked alembic should be placed, to which a larger or royal cucurbit (Herrnkolbe) should be attached as a receiver.

First, therefore, when, with fire gradually applied in stages, the empty cucurbit itself has been heated to incandescence, one spoonful of ground antimony or powder should be gradually and in turns introduced through the tube. It immediately liquefies, and by the force of the fire, the flowers are raised upwards into the superimposed blind alembics. The antimony, once introduced, should be moved frequently through the tube with an iron stylus curved at the end, for thus, indeed, they are carried upwards more quickly and rapidly. All things being properly arranged, the flowers are elevated even to the most distant beaked alembic with a certain portion of acid phlegm, which is to be collected in the attached cucurbit. It is indeed wonderfully effective in expelling worms, taken with water or a decoction of gentian root, 3, 4, or 5 drops; this, therefore, is the method for white flowers.

ANTIMONIAL PILLS
*twofold.*

From white flowers, moreover, very noble pills can be made, which work wonderfully, and for the most part purge through the bowels, often through the upper parts, but then finally more strongly, when the first region of the belly is a mine of impurities, and therefore also, according to the law of indications, has been filled with things to be expelled. This emetic power, however, can easily be removed, leaving only the faculty of purging through the lower parts. Therefore, Antimonial pills are twofold for me: the former are emetic, that is, ἄνω καὶ κάτω (up and down), purging through the lower and upper parts.
   The latter, at least, purge through the bowels. The composition and use of both, hitherto kept secret by me, I faithfully communicate. First of all, let aqua fortis be made from vitriol calcined to yellowness and common salt, of each ℔ iij. To these add double or triple the amount of potter's earth, and mix. Afterwards, from a retort, make the water with a naked fire, then to be freed from phlegm in a Balneum, so that only the spirits, of course, remain. ♃. Then, to the white flowers of antimony, add an equal part of that water, and by means of a Balneum with a slow fire, evaporate the useless phlegm: the spirits, of course, are accumulated with the flowers, and only the aqueous part is sent off. *n* Whether spirit of wine can be used as a suitable menstruum for preparing purgative extracts; the author of *Tyrocinium Chymicum*, book 2, chapter 9, on extracts, discusses this after many others. He believes, however, that in some cases the purgative power, through digestion by spirit of wine, is weakened: but he seems to commit a fallacy; for it does not weaken it, but does not draw it to itself. For the faculty of purgatives resides in volatile mercurial salt: it therefore desires a similar menstruum, whose symbol is the same as that which is to be extracted. But spirit of wine is sulphurous, and retains the nature of sulphur; therefore it attracts from substances that which is of its own nature, namely sulphur; it leaves mercurial salts untouched: it therefore rather serves for the extraction of those whose essence consists in sulphur, such as diaphoretics; but not for purgatives. Nor can their opinion, which attempts to persuade the contrary, namely that no purgative power remains in those to which spirit of wine is added, undermine this opinion of ours; for they say that the cathartic power is indeed extracted by spirit of wi-
                                        ne.

[Another large handwritten 'B' in the left margin]

**CHYMICA. 113**

ni, but that it cannot be easily separated from it, but rather carries it away with itself when it is abstracted. But experience dictates otherwise. For firstly, how can the spirit of wine attract to itself that which is not of its own nature, as just said? Secondly, if it completely extracts the purgative power to itself, that which is not of its own nature, as just said? Then, if it completely extracts the purgative power, how is it that when such an extract, contaminated by this menstruum, has been thoroughly dried, and another suitable [menstruum] is poured on it, it brings forth most effectively into the open the cathartic power still hidden within it? And finally, as for what is added, that the cathartic power cannot be easily separated from the spirit of wine, experience likewise clearly contradicts this. For who will deny that the spirit of wine, when used as a menstruum in an extract of colocynth, can be easily separated from the purgative tincture? Therefore, the purgative power is not fixed in the spirit of wine. For the dregs of purgatives, left behind by the spirit of wine after the extraction process is completed, when afterwards activated by other menstrua, finally yield the purgative power, which was not attracted by the spirit of wine, and which would otherwise be non-existent. 24. Take 2 pounds of crude white Tartar, and pour in a measure of Spirit of wine. With the mouth of the vessel closed, let them digest together in a warm hypocaust for fourteen days. Afterwards, distill with a slow ash fire until yellow oily drops begin to emerge, at which point one must stop. **TRUE PREPARATION OF SOLAR BEZOARDIC.**

*m* Experience and the following reasoning prove that this addition of gold is in no way necessary or useful. Gold, namely, returns to its original body: therefore, it can in no way act nor render the powder of antimony more virtuous. But if gold were truly reduced from its corporeality into a spiritual substance, then its addition would indeed be very useful. If gold is mixed with the Bezoardic itself, even in the smallest amounts, it exerts its powers. But if it truly pleases one to make a Solar Bezoardic, lest the labor and expense be in vain, one must proceed as follows. We will say below, in the first distillation of spirit of nitre, or aqua fortis, that a menstruum of a very reddish transparent color proceeds from the butter itself, and that

This gold, rendered spiritual, when joined to the butter of antimony (dissolved in spirit of nitre or aqua regia) through repeated necessary distillations, can be united with it, and again sealed, and after extreme calcination, prepared into a purple-colored Bezoardic (which is a sign of gold spiritually dissolved and intimately joined), of great virtues in medicine.

that the liquefaction, which Beguinus

that which is more subtle dissolves in the water and

APERITIVE SPIRIT OF TARTAR.
Compounded.

From the simple spirit, extracted from cream of Tartar as previously mentioned, take 1 pound; add 4 ounces of spirit of wine. To this mixture, gradually sprinkle and infuse 2 pounds of vitriol dried to redness with a moderate fire. Digest in a water bath for eight days. Then, drive it off through a retort, applying all degrees of fire. Afterwards, pour all that has come forth over the black caput mortuum of Tartar, from which indeed the simple spirit was made. Digest for 24 hours. Afterwards, separate the water imbued with the Tincture of Tartar by decantation. Calcine the remaining Tartar dregs to whiteness. From these dregs, extract the salt by leaving it in the warm for 24 hours with the previously tinctured water. Purify this water through a filter. And they administer it with great success for stubborn obstructions of the viscera, for foul complexions, chronic fevers, and dropsy, from 1 dram to 2 drams in appropriate waters.

SULPHUR OR TRUE TINCTURE
OF TARTAR.

First, therefore, the most purified Salt of Tartar is prepared, which is finally obtained by frequent solutions, coagulations, and fusions: This, highly purified, is melted in a strong crucible with a strong fire, and kept in a molten state for so long until it changes from a green color to blue, of such acrimony and corrosiveness that, when applied to the tongue, it burns like fire. It is extracted by homogeneous spirit of wine, specifically, by pouring it slowly, not all at once, to a height of 3 fingers, and leaving it for some time in the cold, but afterwards gently boiling it in ashes, and repeating this extraction as long as the operation is possible. But when the spirit of wine has been separated by distillation, there remains a red liquid like blood, of a most fragrant odor, which finally, with fresh spirit of wine to the height of one finger

As a concluding remark for the third and fourth
Diaphoretic, I add transparent gold, which
they also call "perspectible" by a plainly
barbaric name, as well as Panacea composed
from antimony sulfur; that is translucent
antimony glass, to which gold has been added
by infusion.

gold, from which mixture and transparency it
received that name. The preparation is as follows.
Recipe. Of purest gold ½ ounce. Of Hungarian
antimony 8 ounces. Place in a crucible over fire, so that they may
melt together, and when it is melted, pour it out; Be careful,
however, that it does not turn into a regulus. Grind this mixture
thoroughly and well, so that a very fine powder is made,
which is to be calcined in the same way that
antimony is calcined when they wish to
make glass, until it no longer fumes.
When therefore you have the powder thus fixed,
place the crucible over the fire, so that it glows intensely
so that it may turn into glass; Afterwards, gradually in that
manner pour the powder into the glass, and let it flow
for so long, until this glass is red and transparent,
which you can test with some iron rod.
And you will find the gold at the bottom of the
crucible diminished by half. Pour the glass into a
basin, and you will have transparent gold
mixed with antimony glass of equal weight.
Take of this transparent gold,
powdered as desired, and pour onto it
spirit of wine made from wine and very well rectified,
to the height of 4 fingers, and in a closed
vessel set aside at digestive heat, and the
spirit will extract from the gold a very red
Tincture, which you will reserve for use. This

PANACEA OF ANTIMONY SULPHUR.

The true sulphur of antimony is like a panacea, joined and fixed with the regulus of antimony, melted and made in the manner already mentioned for transparent gold. It certainly has a diaphoretic power in itself, and therefore can serve to properly and correctly expel any diseases from the body. The preparation is as follows. From cinnabar of antimony, as described above for the flowers of butter of anti-

--- Page 201 ---
CHYMICA. 191

antimony, after the distilled butter, let red sulfur be skillfully extracted in this manner: Let a very strong lye be made from potash and quicklime, equal parts, as is customary; with this, first accurately purified and filtered, powdered cinnabar of antimony should boil for 3 or 4 hours: the lye turns reddish, and the quicksilver flows freely at the bottom of the vessel. The tinted lye, separated by decantation and still warm, filtered through blotting paper, should rest for 8 hours or more; and thus the sulfur of antimony will settle to the bottom in the form of a red powder, which, separated from the lye, must be washed repeatedly with common water, then dried with gentle heat. Of this [sulfur of antimony] and Regulus of antimony, 1 dram each. Of oil of sulfur made by the bell, 1 ounce, or of oil of Vitriol, 3 drams. Digest for several days in a glass retort in a warm place, then distill in a sand bath, cohobating three times; press the last time with a fourth-degree fire for 12 hours, and the whole will remain fixed in the fire. Of this, 1 ounce. Of salt or Magistery of corals, 2 drams. Mix thoroughly and let a powder be made. Dose from 10 to 15 and 20 grains. Repeat the administration often in any diseases, especially in epidemic diseases and those carrying some malignancy. See also the Chymiatric Practice of our edition, p. 14.

Of pearl preparations, very many are found, and especially their salt, prepared according to the mind of our author, does not lack its exquisite virtue. Nor indeed for that reason do we despise the common preparation of pearls. From these, thus prepared, are those two compositions in the workshops of Diamargaritum, namely hot and cold. Thus indeed they are commonly prepared: Purged from impurities, washed with water of roses, carnations, melissa, and violets, they are ground for some time on a porphyry stone without the aid of any metal, until they are levigated, precisely in the manner which painters observe in levigating their colors. But through this levigation, even a laborious one, they cannot reduce the pearls into such minute particles that they seem to have shed all their corpulence. Therefore, chymists desire and investigate that elaboration which can better exert its greatest powers, namely such as are: The Salt of which the author speaks, the Magistery, the Fifth Essence.    **SECOND METHOD OF TINCTURE**
            **OF CORALS.**

Another Tincture, superior to the former, although that solvent extracts Tincture from corals, it is nevertheless rather from distilled vinegar than from the corals themselves. This therefore, because not pure, can scarcely satisfy a medical purpose. Therefore, another method must be investigated, by which Tincture can be elegantly extracted from corals; and it is as follows: First, the corals are calcined, not pulverized, but whole, with a reverberatory fire, first slow, so that at least a living flame touches the corals placed in dishes (earthen saucers) in a reverberatory furnace, only on the surface. The corals in this way first whiten, and hide their native color. Therefore, the body of the corals must be fatigued for so long by successively increasing degrees of fire, until from whiteness to yellowness, and from yellow-

Thus, if corals prepared in this way are introduced into spirit of wine, or into the alcohol of the spirit of May dew (lily of the valley), a little later they spontaneously deposit their tincture into that same alcohol, with the dregs remaining at the bottom without any virtue. One bowl receives the oil of camphor: into this let the calx of gold be placed, and at the same time let the oil of cloves be poured in; immediately all will be seen to boil and bubble. Therefore, immediately, from that bowl into the other; by pouring back and forth, let the entire mixture be poured and repoured, so that, when they are seen to grow hot and boil, the calx of gold may be mixed with them, and as if dissolved during the boiling: for all things become very red and thick, like blood. While these things are being completed by pouring back and forth, next let the remaining oils also be added, and, by pouring back and forth repeatedly, let all be mixed diligently. N.B. The glass bowls, as well as the oils required for this operation, must be entirely free from any watery phlegm; otherwise, the process itself would not succeed. Therefore, Thurneisserus held this composition as a great secret, and sold it very dearly, namely, half an ounce for 18 Imperials. But the Hermetic Philosopher considers this empirical and crude operation worthy of reproach: for it is fal-

--- Page 232 ---
222      B A S I L I C A
deceptive and exceedingly alien from the truth. Camphor indeed is reduced by aqua fortis into an oily liquid: for at the same time it contains within itself the spirits of that aqua fortis: therefore it is not truly oil. Now therefore when this liquid is mixed with other fatty oils, a mutual ebullition occurs, which is not from elsewhere than from the spirits of the salts of aqua fortis, otherwise reacting in a similar way with other oils due to their contrary nature: therefore little and almost nothing of the Sun (gold) is dissolved at the same time; or, if anything is dissolved, it is not done by any of the oils; but merely by the corrosive spirits themselves, mutually heated by the oils. Furthermore, the same oils, mixed and blended among themselves without Solar calx, in the way we said, subsequently become thick and red: this redness therefore is from them, not directly from gold. What good therefore is to be hoped from such deceptions is now clear. It is therefore probable that our author wished at least to warn in passing that little and nothing should be attributed to these things, and not to defend such great foolishness.

**COMFORTING BALMS**
a Thickened by means of wax.

*Because aromatic oils in liquid form cannot be carried around suitably and conveniently due to the danger of spilling or the breaking of glass, Chymists began to think about a method of thickening them, so that their various preparations could be carried around more conveniently in tin or silver boxes (but properly gilded), and be at hand in urgent necessity.*
*However, for preparing these, it is sufficient for this time to have at least hinted to the diligent that for each preparation is required both an oil drawn out by distillation and a Tincture extracted by rectified spirit (Spiritus vini Alcoholisatum) and thickened by separation from the same Spirit: Also, a Salt drawn out after incineration by the agency of water from its caput mortuum: A medium, which gives the proper consistency, rasu-*

    a Comforting Balms are nothing else than compounded aromatic oils, made thicker by the addition of other things which serve as bases, so that they may indeed be carried around and retained more suitably. But concerning the composition of these balms, it is disputed whether a certain weight of principles should or even can be observed throughout. We deny it. For some are indeed drier and have a completely dry Tincture, such as cinnamon; some have very oily Tinctures, such as nutmeg, mace, fennel, anise, cloves; some obtain a moderate nature, such as ginger. Therefore, according to whether their natures are drier and more arid, the weight of the oil also varies accordingly. In general, however, only so much of the consistent base is mixed in as suffices for the thickening of the oil, by which it may afterwards be mixed with the tincture more successfully. BALSAM OF FENNEL.

♃. Of Tincture of Fennel made from the seed with spirit of wine 3 ounces.

Melt the wax, very well cleaned and thinly scraped, with a gentle heat of fire; to the melted wax add the oil, and mix outside the fire, stirring with an iron spatula, until it solidifies; afterwards add the Tincture extracted with spirit of wine, and mix again. When all things have now been brought to their consistency and have cooled, add 1/2 dram of Fennel salt to each ounce of the whole compound, which makes 2 drams, and thus let it be kept for use. But because wax becomes rancid with age, and thus imparts an unpleasant taste to such compositions, moreover, [according to] Galen in book 7 on the faculties of medicines, [wax is] of an emplastic nature and a thick essence that prohibits perspiration; therefore it also closes the pores, and with the pores closed, it is necessary that an ineffective operation of the balsams follows; and an ineffective operation is followed only by an ineffective effect. ANTEPILEPTIC CONFECTION
By Paracelsus.

First, from three human skulls, not buried but violently killed and dried in the air, somewhat coarsely crushed, a liquid is distilled from a retort with a slow sand fire into a capacious receiver; afterwards, with increasing observed degrees (of heat), a fire of suppression can be applied. This liquid he extracts by distilling it a third time over the same dregs, and finally rectifies it through an alembic. Of this liquid, he takes 7 or 8 ounces. He adds 1/2 ounce of the species of sweet Diamuscus, and of Castoreum and Anacardium honey, 3 ounces of each. And in turn, he distills it from ashes through a retort. Finally, he adds 4 ounces of liquor of pearls, and 1 ounce of oil of vitriol, or rather, of the antiepileptic spirit prescribed above. From this entire mixture, he administered one spoonful daily to a person suffering from epilepsy, on an empty stomach, continuing for nine days. It is reported that Paracelsus performed wonders with this unique remedy. Therefore, he communicated it to the Emperor who sought it, but asked that these things not be revealed to makers of syrups. 8. To the same Paracelsus is also attributed the essence of human skull, which, because of its mucilaginous substance, he was accustomed to call 'Galreda of human skull'; others call it Gelatin.

**OIL OF AMBER.**

In preparing this, uncommon diligence is required, for it demands a suitable and proper fire. We use white Amber, generated from the purest and unmixed Bitumen in the sea, in medicine, not the yellow kind a.

♃. Therefore, take fragments of white Amber (for example, 2 or 3 pounds) and pound them coarsely; do not grind them into a fine powder. First, if necessary, wash away impurities with common water. Then place them in a cucurbit or alembic not too tall, and pour in a good quantity of Rose and Betony water b (which is done so that the Oil is not burned, and so that by means of these waters it may begin to distill more easily). Place a capacious head with a sufficiently wide beak, and adapt a receiving vessel. And in sand, with the glass joints sealed on both sides as is customary, maintaining a suitable and continuous degree of fire lest it cool down (otherwise it blackens like pitch and breaks the glass), let the distillation be completed. Also, be careful lest the fire become too strong, otherwise the receiver is endangered.

First, water and white oil emerge with spirits like clouds. Then no more visible spirit emerges, but streaks appear in the head, as is seen in the distillation of Spirit of wine. Finally, yellow oil comes: here one must stop S from de-

CONTINUATION OF A PURER
POTABLE GOLD.

This very solution of the calx of the Sun by oil of salt, and finally the expulsion of the same with spirit of urine through a retort, is neither necessary nor even safe enough. Therefore, we leave the author to his own opinion; nevertheless, for a more genuine preparation to be undertaken more safely, we will proceed as follows. That calx of the Sun, previously reduced to the highest brightness by extreme reverberation, let it be dissolved with a menstruum also previously completely perfected from spirit of urine and spirit of wine. Let it be dissolved, I say, in slow heat into a solution reddening like blood. This solution is then digested in a hermetically sealed vessel for a month. After the solution is finally separated from the dregs, and the menstruum or solvent spirit is finally drawn off by the heat of a very slow Balneum (Mariae) – which can then be used for the same purposes again and is almost perpetually sufficient – the Sun (gold) remains in the form of a very red oil, spreading a sweet odor from itself, and soluble in any liquid; therefore, this oil can take the place of true potable gold and be its substitute. Furthermore, the same (oil) is exalted or rendered purer, when, namely, the solar spirit is separated from its body,

HERMAPHRODITIC VITRIOL.

First, let oil of vitriol be made, such as was made above, in its spirit, and such as is now made for a stomachic purpose. Let a suitable quantity of this be made. Then prepare elegant iron filings, not dusty, nor rusty, but freshly made: upon these, however, pour some oil of vitriol as desired, yet not too much. **LIQUID OF JUPITER.**
*Crystals of Jupiter (Tin) for the same medication of suffocations, and other things, can be made more refined in the following way. Take English Tin; dissolve in aqua fortis, which is made from niter and alum, and a little later pour in the tin itself; the aqua fortis appears in the manner of a whitish lime. Dry this lime, and through pots placed over a tubulated cucurbit below, sublimate it in the manner that it is otherwise usually done with white flowers of antimony; and thus the spirit of tin is carried upwards, in the form of a very white powder or flour. Dissolve this powder in distilled vinegar, and extra-*

**CHYMICA. 347**
**FLOWERS OF SULFUR.**

Crude sulfur should have no use in medicine, unless that which is found in mines and is called "Scissile" (or "Cleavable") is at hand, purified by Nature, which is not at all contrary to flowers of sulfur prepared by art. For just as here by artificial Fire, so there by Natural (process), the finer part of sulfur is raised to higher places, and for that reason is more thoroughly refined. Therefore, when scissile (sulfur) is at hand, it is permitted to use it in place of Flowers. But because Nature rarely supplies us with an abundance of scissile (sulfur), Chymical physicians began to think about a method by which they might be relieved in its scarcity.

In the Cracovian region in Poland, it is seen purified by a wonderful art of Nature, and formerly in the Neapolitan Kingdom near Puteoli, where a sulfurous mountain perpetually burns, I saw it with great interest. [Marginal note: Vesuvius, a mountain of Campania.] In that place, sulfur is accustomed to exude from the rocks like dew. That Flower is most pure, which if it were available in abundance, a true Spagyricist could extract from it a unique medicine for himself by Chymical mastery.

Sulfur, however, is produced there, after it is separated from stones and Earth by the force of fire.

Near Salzburg, in copper mines, where they extract Vitriol from the ore, by "roasting," as they call it, sulfur is accustomed to fly away from the ore, which then usually adheres to the furnace like pollen, for receiving and retaining this smoke stu-

OTHER ZENEXTA.

To the number of periaptos or amulets, hung from the neck in time of plague, proposed by the author, others are added, which indeed do not change the type or material; yet they differ from them in preparation. There is indeed great ingenuity of the human mind, striving to change the same things into different forms, and thereby demonstrating its nobility. It was said from the beginning that quicksilver in a hollowed-out hazelnut, and afterwards exactly closed, hung from the neck, earned the principal name of Zenextum; afterwards, arsenic was included in the same category. Both can, the material remaining the same, be reduced to a more suitable form, concerning which it must be held thus, and indeed first concerning Mercury.

METHOD OF PREPARING SALTS
*Crystalline from Vegetables or transparent like Nitre.*

4. Calcine or burn the ashes of any vegetable with an equal part of elegant sulfur in powder, using a fire not very gentle; thus all lixivious greasiness perishes from the ashes with the sulfur. From these ashes, finally, with common or proper water, extract the salt, distilling the extractions until a pellicle forms, and afterwards depositing it in the cold to crystallize. As much sulfur as ashes is to be taken. These salts are the best of all.

I have observed the following method of preparation:
1. The five gums (a), macerated in vinegar and boiled, should be pressed through a thick linen cloth twice, repeating the boiling. (The dose of the gums can be increased because of the dregs remaining from the pressing and to be discarded.) Afterwards, over a slow heat in a clean pan (i) they are thickened until a medium consistency.
2. Linseed oil and olive oil should be placed in another pan, and Litharge of Gold and Silver should be added. They should be boiled, stirring, until the oil is colored. Afterwards, Calamine should be added, and a little later Minium. All of these, stirring for almost two hours, should be boiled together sufficiently, of which the proof is, if a drop solidifies and condenses on the fingernail, and no longer flows away.
3. Finally, also, towards the end, Vernix, Laurel oil, Wax, Colophony should be added. All having been well mixed together and liquefied, and from the fire

In the shins or legs, erysipelas easily yields if skillfully made linen bandages are used. But these should be soaked seven times or even more with the same sperniola, and as if shaken with it, and then dried again. These, indeed, can last for many years, provided they are not wiped or cleaned with other water. From their use, erysipelas neither returns so easily nor is it repelled with such difficulty, but rather, immediately from the beginning of the application, both pain and swelling with redness cease.

# EPILOGUE.

*Let the supercilious Academic Thrasos, revilers of Chymists' Medicines, cease now and henceforth. These are the ones who, with threats and violent rebukes, deciding by their own authority, have hitherto foolishly mocked, condemned, and subjected to a thousand insults the faithful Truth of our ancestors and divine science. Let them cease, I say, to brand the disciples of Hermes with the marks of infamy, envy, ignorance, and fraud, and henceforth to demand ocular demonstrations and clear methods of operations. Likewise, let them cease to imperiously demand Spagyric secrets from the 'Carbonarii,' as they call them, physicians, by their unusual and new method of learning. Secrets which, inspired by divine Virtue, I have candidly communicated to the Republic in full measure this time.*

*Meanwhile, I earnestly implore this one thing from the fiercest Avenger of all Falsehood and Injustice: that to all who, with ardent invocation of the aid of Almighty God and a grateful heart, will rightly use these preparations for the praise and glory of the Creator, for the sincere and due benefit of the needy neighbor, and for the undeservedly proclaimed honor of the Chymical art; and who, acknowledging God's generosity, will attribute these benefits to the Spagyric Commonwealth – may He grant and bestow upon them Grace and all Blessing in healing. To the mocker-*

--- Page 479 ---
C H Y M I C A. 469
But to unworthy scoffers, and to those who, with feigned contempt, shall secretly use these gifts of God (just as it is manifest that hitherto many idle Galenists have done, seeking praise and esteem for themselves rightly from the labors of others), and who with internal perfidy shall not cease to persecute Spagyric benefactors either by word or deed, may all things turn out contrary. And that this may be firm and ratified, may that most Holy TRINITY grant, who gave me the will and ability to consecrate these Chymical labors, and these Spagyric grains, threshed from the chaff, most thoroughly and most often examined not without the greatest studies, to the memory of perpetual posterity, and may the entire Spagyric Senate and People say with me from the bottom of their hearts, Amen.
  Live, Farewell, Reader, if you know anything more correct than these things,
  Impart it candidly: if not, use these gratefully.

Platonic doctrines, in their course, will return to their followers complete, and clothed in a far more splendid adornment, freely, than I had once received the same, half-torn and for a price, from their authors. For among some, to whom the rumor of many hidden secrets had drawn me with the tedious difficulties and expenses of journeys, their very presence, as often happens, diminished their fame: so that what they presented as secrets then seemed to me either commonplace, or mutilated and incomplete, whose deficiencies I had to supply from many descriptions reduced by me into one, nevertheless first proving the same by the test of fire itself; by an exchange also not harmful to them, according to that well-known Chymical custom, (καὶ δὸς τὶ, καὶ λαβὲ τὶ – and give something, and take something) while I often compared my studies with them, they received an egg for a nut in mutual conversation, which [nut], broken by long, laborious, and vain efforts, I finally found to be a rotten kernel, or instead of a kernel, mere husks and pods.

--- Page 497 ---
**ADMONITORIA. 7**

By labors, then, they had spent a very long time. Those who, not content with my example and the harm of others, will prefer hereafter to examine such things by the ministry of pyrotechnics and Chemistry, and to become more cautious at their own peril, will willingly admit with me that the matter stands thus. And just as there are many things in words which are not found in deeds, so many things are lost between Theory and practice. He will experience (it), who desires to make another's danger his own, and to be deceived by those who have been deceived by others. [Marginal note: Learn to beware by the warnings of others, lest you regret the labor expended.] Therefore, in this study, no one should be trusted further than what each person finds proven by his own experience, by touching and seeing, through the proper test of fire, distinguishing the false from the true. And because, according to Aeschylus, he is at last considered wise ὁ χρήσιμα, οὐχ ὁ πολλ᾽ εἰδὼς (he who knows useful things, not he who knows many things), I preferred to offer fewer and more select things, frequently revolving in my mind that saying of Damascenus: You should hold few medicines, whose powers and operation you have often experienced. Nevertheless, in this small number, I can confidently assert to you that in the majesty and storehouse of all Nature (if you except that universal and most celebrated Medicine possessed by the wisest Philosophers from the world's foundation, and sung down to a miracle to its legitimate heirs) [Marginal note: See Anaxagoras in his book 'On Natural Things'.] scarcely anything lies hidden that is more select and more efficacious than these principal Arcana of more secret medicine now offered, οὐδ᾽ ἐν τῷ μεγάλῳ τὸ εὖ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ εὖ τὸ μέγα (nor is the good in the great, but the great in the good). But since virtue is always seen wounded by the goads of Envy, and Envy is the companion of those who make progress and study for the public good: indeed, not even Jupiter, whether he rains or is clear, pleases everyone, and it is most difficult to be able to render grateful service to an ungrateful world, these are worthy of mercy rather than anger, until they someday free themselves spontaneously from the tormenting Purgatory of their envy.

for their own Reasons do not seek, especially lest, with the truth revealed, they be bound by an academic oath to swear by the errors of the heathen Scholastic Gods, and to die in them. And these indeed, masked Titles, even if formerly by a laudable institution they were a spur to virtue and a deserved reward for erudition, today however, especially in the medical faculty, they are conferred upon many most unworthy individuals, either by prayer or by * price (I am not speaking of those who obtain the just Titles and laurels of their Degree by the merits of their doctrine) who, after being about to give proof of their studies in the first two or three years, have experienced the potter's craft in the loss of such a noble vessel, proceeding according to their method which excuses all errors, whether the patient lives or dies, finally in the fourth, fifth, and subsequent years, they perceive the insufficiency and lack of erudition required in a physician, even to the disgrace of their own name, and with remorse of conscience. And then they ought rightly to doubt whether even Galen's Theorems, destined for us no less, as he writes, than for bears and wild boars, and his Methods of medicine, established by no authority of antiquity, by which our age triumphs, would have a good foundation, because they are ocularly convinced that the end does not correspond to its beginning in the great cures of diseases. While however they consider the writings of other good men as nothing,

--- Page 507 ---
**ADMONITORIA. 17**

Certain Theophrastians, who have more fully and more thoroughly investigated the causes of hidden things, are accustomed to add a Fourth, which they call Spirit, [marginal note: The Spirit of the Lord upon the waters.] which, although it can be obtained from minerals and vegetables, nevertheless in animals, because of its subtlety, it is not subjected to the actions of the artisan, nor can it be captured: thus Sulphur would correspond to Fire, Salt to Earth, Mercury to Water, Spirit to Air.

And because we have fallen into mention of the Elements, we will subjoin these few things about them from the concise tradition of Severinus: The true Elements are plainly spiritual guardians, nurses, places, mines, matrices, and receptacles of the whole Creation: indeed, the essence, existence, life, and actions of all Beings.

But the places of Things are not idle, but endowed with their own properties, which exhibit life and nourishment to their inhabitants, that is, to seeds, so that they may bring forth from themselves what they observe hidden in their treasures and innermost parts.

how Medicine acts in the human body,

As to what physicians commonly dispute, whether according to Hippocrates' oracle Opposites are the Remedies for Opposites, or truly according to Paracelsus Likes for Likes, it must be observed that the expressions of these two axioms, although seemingly dissimilar in appearance and contradictory, are admitted in the Anatomy of Nature. Thus many do not grasp the mind of the Philosophers, because they do not understand that what appears to be discord among them is a beautiful harmony, if the disagreement is reconciled by timely and consistent interpretation. For Medicine is nothing else
                                                                    ...

--- Page 599 ---
**ADMONITORIA. 109**
is nothing else than the opposition of those things which are lacking, namely the restoration of strength and Balsam, and the removal of those things which are redundant, namely morbid impurities. Therefore Paracelsus does not oppose Hippocrates, who asserts that hunger is cured by food, thirst by drink, repletion by evacuation, inanition by restoration, labor by rest, rest by labor; and universally that Contraries are the Remedies of Contraries. But he manifestly opposes Galen, who especially adapts Hippocratic Contrariety to those bare qualities condemned by Hippocrates, for by an unhappy error he refers the primary and principal Ideas of Cures to refrigerations, calefactions, humectations, exsiccations, and their accomplices.

The Natures of Remedies alone, as said above, or Hippocratic *dynameis*, are the healers of diseases, but the physician is a minister. And this same Nature, namely our Life and Balsam or Balsamic Mumia, defending the body from any Corruption, through the medium of the Saline liquor, that is, the inferior Balsam, born from the superior within the inferiors—this same Nature of ours, I say (which sometimes performs miracles, the help of physicians having been implored in vain, physicians who, to the great disgrace of their name and the dishonor of the medical art, had too prematurely given up the patient with their prognostics)—is the proper physician of the Human body to itself, who requires nothing else from an extrinsic physician, except for Restoration, or as they commonly say, fortification, exter-

--- Page 600 ---
110          PREFACE

Thence it reassumes the weakened Natural forces, which, once recovered, it is powerful by itself,
[marginal note: Nature cures with similars.]
as an internal and congenital Antidote, to drive all its enemies from its monarchy, by the sole virtue of the Vital faculties: To wish to cure sick bodies with contrary qualities is nothing else than to stir up an intrinsic war, leading to the total ruin of a Nature already sufficiently weakened by internal war: Add to this that contraries do not mutually receive each other. And if they do not mutually receive each other, neither do they mutually act upon each other, nor do they mutually suffer anything from each other: where therefore true action and passion is not present, there also a true Natural effect does not follow. Therefore, medicines cannot be contrary to the affected place, but it is necessary that they be most akin to it, and have the same External Nature (because of the Harmony of macrocosm and microcosm) that this affected place has Internally, so that the deficient Internal Nature of that place may be both strengthened and helped by the superabundance of that External Nature: Therefore it is called Microcosm, because the whole world preserves, nourishes, and cures man: For when the fruits of Earth, Air, Water, Fire of the Microcosm sicken, it is necessary that they be restored by similar fruits of the Macrocosm.

be restored: And thus Nature strengthens and helps its own Nature: But Nature, strengthened and helped by its own Nature, strongly expels every enemy of its own, since naturally every Nature is most preservative of itself: And thus we have Nature not only as an ally, but as a friendly and helpful assistant, since she alone is the genuine healer of all diseases, as Galen also testifies in his thirteenth book of Method. The prime mover of all healing, since without whose strength or vigor all medicine is useless and in vain. Nature preserved in its own Temperament is medicine in itself, and it heals its own infirmities through its innate Mummia: and where this Internal Nature refuses to be medicine, there all diseases are lethal. For this is too well known, that every thing by a certain natural instinct desires to be perfected and preserved: Conversely, it most vehemently abhors its own destruction, and avoids it as much as possible: The parts of our body injured by a sword or in any other way, prove this to us by daily experience: For the injured feel the immediate help of Nature, as if rushing to their aid, and so tireless, that it will not rest until, having overcome the disfiguring wound, it has restored the injured parts to their pristine integrity. And after, from the apprehension of undoubted death that would follow, as if half-dead, he had lodged the said knife in his stomach for seven whole weeks and two days, by the use and aid of Attracting Plasters made from Magnet and other things, its point, by natural impulse, began to attempt an exit near the opening of the stomach. Which having been detected, it was instantly requested by the patient (although many were dissuading the act because of the imminent danger to life) that it should be extracted by incision. Which was finally obtained by entreaties from the chief surgeon of the Kingdom and city, Florian Matthis of Brandenburg, on Thursday after the feast of Pentecost at seven in the morning, however, for an outcome of all fortune and doubtful health.

The color of the excised knife, nine inches long, now deposited among the Emperor's rarer possessions (having been shown to many people, both in the Emperor's court and in the city, as an incredible miracle), was so changed in the stomach as if it had lain in fire during that time. The rustic, within a few weeks, with legitimate remedies applied by an expert surgeon, without any further illness or discomfort, always eating well, drinking, and sleeping, as he often reported to me, by God's help and the generosity of many towards the poor man, contrary to the determined assertion of medical aphorisms, completely recovered his former health, free of charge, and a little later celebrated his wedding. Similarly, in the year 1606, a certain Silesian in Prague, having received money in the presence of many people, swallowed white flints collected by the riverbank, forty-six in number, weighing nearly three medicinal pounds, the smallest of which equaled the size of a pigeon's egg, and all of which could barely be grasped by me with four handfuls. With this reckless daring, for several years, he made a living here and there in the city without detriment to his health, etc.

V. THE OFFICE OF THE PHYSICIAN, MINISTER OF NATURE.

Just as the term "vulgar philosophy" is not attributed to Aristotle, as is solidly shown—

[Marginal note: A wavy vertical line is drawn in ink in the right margin, spanning from approximately the third line to the twenty-fifth line of the main text block.]

--- Page 610 ---

P. Ramus demonstrated: thus not even the whole Light of Nature, as Paracelsus testifies, is exhausted in Galen alone. Men ought not to deprive other men of the freedom of human intellect, the Light of Nature, the faculty of discerning and judging, for the Monarchy of the Greeks has ceased. Therefore, whoever desires to excel in the medical art (since no one can truly become learned who swears by the rudiments of only one faculty) ought to be independent of every kind of sect, nor swear by the opinion of any author, but only follow the naked Truth, and subscribe to it, always mindful of that Horatian [verse]:
   Wherever the storm carries me, I am borne as a guest.
   Bound to swear by the words of no master.
Nor are the discoveries of others, by adhering to one sect, to be universally rejected, but all sects, whatever they are, are to be familiarly acknowledged, since, according to the noblest and wisest phoenix of philosophers, Pico della Mirandola, an inimitable example of profound intellect and manifold erudition, in each family [school of thought] there is something remarkable, which is not common to it with the others: No book is so bad and abject that it does not contain something good, often neglected by the most excellent authors: A later age, says Fabius, has labored more to educate itself than the former, and while the sciences themselves [all hidden things by divine order] grow with intellects, many of the most shameful errors of the Pagans, Afterwards a wiser progeny, tan-

He was remarkably skilled in the Chymical Art, yet he is not its author: [Marginal note: This Philosophy flourished among all peoples.] There is a great number of Philosophers who, using their intellect and memory instead of books, became famous through it before Theophrastus was born, and from whom Paracelsus tacitly borrowed many things: For that renowned Pyronomical Art was most ancient, undeservedly defamed by the ignorant, once very well known especially to Kings, Princes, and a few very diligent investigators of Natural Philosophy; nevertheless, it received no small increase through Paracelsus himself, the Monarch of Secrets: And because, by a certain fatal depravity and negligence of times and men, the doctrine of Antiquity, lost and obliterated for many years—namely, the True and Philosophical Medicine, hitherto attempted to be restored by no one in his time—he, by singular Divine providence and impulse, attempted to bring forth from darkness into light, to restore, to expand, and to unfold and illustrate its great obscurity, and to cleanse it from feigned deceit and the mask of imposture; nay, by a certain divine coupling, he attempted to recall the entire harmony of sciences and muses from the whole circumference of the circle to a single center: [Marginal note: A physician created by God can do all things.] Behold, the Devil, the perpetual enemy of the human race and of emerging truth—

[Marginal note: James ch. 1, sect. 17.]
enemy and inseparable malicious companion, also stirred up his emissaries and satellites, and still today incites them, who, with a certain dog-like Envy, strive to keep others from the food which they themselves are not permitted to enjoy, and begrudge that singular good to human necessities: And I know not whether it was done with greater impiety than blasphemy, that the singular gifts of the physician born of Theophrastus's peculiar influence, in curing the most desperate diseases, which they ought to ascribe to the accustomed Author of medicine (from whom, as from the Father of Lights, comes every good and perfect Gift) with humble thanksgiving and due reverence, these things, out of the virulence of their spirit against Truth, in the manner of the Pharisees, they attributed to the malignant Devil himself as if he were the effector (whom they make more powerful than the Omnipotent, [even though he is] bound by His rope, deprived of the Light of Grace and Nature by a benevolent and glorious God), not only with impious and sacrilegious audacity, but also with nefarious and inexpiable wickedness: Those things are to be ascribed to God alone, as the author of the universe and of Nature, and of her Law, which they do not hesitate to attribute to that Devil, to whom, however, no power is granted over the will or intellect of Man: And thus they worship Demons instead of God, blaspheming the Glory, Goodness, and Omnipotence of GOD, and obscuring His Wisdom or Image hidden in man with malicious ignorance. Our German physicians ought not to be so injurious to their homeland, Germany, and despise the gifts granted to their Nature.

**ADMONITORY. 127**

Divinely granted Arcana are neglected: for they only seek and praise what is not their own, but rather alien, and suppress their own with a certain base spirit, just as it also happened to P. Ramus, lamenting the impediment to the youth in the progress of their studies, at the hands of his envious countrymen in simple, common, and corruptible philosophy. For just as the Aristotelians unjustly rose up against him, so also the common doctors rose up against Theophrastus Paracelsus, whose erudition foreign nations rightly admire and are astonished by. Not content with their own medical province, sending their sickle into another's harvest, they did not hesitate to cavil at his theological writings, which they had neither seen, nor read, nor understood due to the poverty of their own intellect (although only the Intellect, seized by the inspiration of divine Wisdom, judges Truth), in which he fruitlessly attempted to manifest to an ungrateful and unworthy world the most invincible Foundation, drawn from the Book of Grace and Nature, of combined Theological and Philosophical Truth and perfect Piety, namely, that our mind might be elevated to God, and our eyes raised to seek Truth, and through Regeneration to the desire for future Beatitude. For without Philosophy, to be supremely pious is plainly impossible [ἀδύνατον]: nor will anyone ever be able to philosophize supremely and Christianly in both Lights, who is not truly pious: For two Lights are known, within which are All things, outside which is Nothing, and no perfect

**ADMONITIONS. 131**

[Marginal note, top right:]
Our condition is a falling away from unity to otherness.

[Marginal note, middle right, partially struck through:]
Seneca: As often as I was among men, I always returned home a lesser man.

[Marginal note, lower right:]
O how difficultly do those become foolish who have once immersed themselves in human wisdom.

Nature and proper quality neglected, God abandoned, through a deviant error, as if proprietors, we slide into ourselves or into creatures in vain, and necessarily fall back into Evil or our own Nothingness: For if the soul returns within itself and is converted into Mind, it approaches God, sees all things, and has no need of external discipline, in the manner of Angels, who learn, hear, and see all things from within: Turned towards the senses, it is estranged from God, and the impure departs from the pure, from God. The academic spirit cannot grasp this mystery: for only Pious and Religious Humility, the noblest of virtues, is capable of Illumination. But since this Truth cannot be comprehended unless our Intellect is inflamed by the Word of the Lord, and Reason receives Divine Light through the Mind, and since it is not right to speak more publicly about these mysteries in this unsuitable place, I return from the digression into which a just reason had led me, to Paracelsus the physician.

Our physicians, however, ought to embrace such great Gifts of God in him, and rather to love the man (whom it is easier to hate [μισεῖν] than to imitate [μιμεῖσθαι]) for his most ingenious art, than to hate him for his manners and words not obvious to all. The age should excuse the barbarity of his writings; malicious ingratitude of men [should excuse] the deplorable obscurity of his commentaries; the strange custom of philosophers [should excuse] the unheard-of novelty of names—[philosophers] who, a lazy herd born to gnaw at the industry of others, from the most holy scien-

132          PREFACE
of the most sacred sciences they have always kept away, according to that saying of Plato,
   *That arts may be hidden, and grow through their own enigmas.*
   The rights of mastery and liberties have been everywhere conceded.
   Let anyone reflect inwardly, if he had possessed what Theophrastus knew, would he want to tell this to all men? He would act against the oath of Hippocrates, who also did not want to teach medicine to everyone. Indeed, a secret must be hidden, which is granted to God alone to reveal, and which, if divulged, is accustomed to bring either death or imprisonment or ignominy, or at least continuous fear and voluntary exile (unless by lying and defrauding, for the sake of covering themselves, they wish to brand their name with a perpetual stain) far from one's country and one's own people for the sake of security, just as, besides the examples of more recent times, those of Lullus himself, Arnold, Zacharias of Paris, and others testify. True Hermetic Philosophers established an oath, that they would imitate the footsteps of their fathers and teachers, and would not with any rashness profane the virginity of Nature, preserved from the beginning of ages:
[Without labor, no one ought to possess the art.] To sworn disciples, however, and those bound by perpetual gratitude and faith, dignified by Nature or by Instruction, they gave precepts, still to be elucidated with much sweat. **ADMONITIONS. 133**
(Continuing from the previous page: ...he spares) no kind of physicians, and professes himself the sole and unique physician of the world. He at least condemns the common crowd of physicians, unskilled in both Theory and Practice; and indeed, those are not to be considered physicians who, while accomplishing nothing by healing, merely wrangle verbosely and syllogistically about medical matters, which is a sign of foolish ambition, and claim the method of medicine for themselves, a class of men swollen with arrogance and pride, and born to suppress the truth of the Medical Art.

Among whom some (since repentance of revocation is utterly adverse to the proud and inexperienced) are so disposed towards Theophrastus himself, that they would rather a patient die than use medicines prescribed by him; many also despise his medicines for this reason, lest if these are openly used, and their wonderful effect is observed, something of their own authority should diminish for them; and thus, the better they are, the more contemptible they are to them.

And although Theophrastus's deceitful Methodic censors (who, by postponing remedies, prolong illness for their own gain) accuse genuine Chymists of having abandoned the true method, it is groundless, since that [method] which Paracelsus follows is consistent with both Reason and Experience, as is manifest to those endowed with the Light of Understanding: Nor ought we to be so devoted to any authority that we do not prefer Truth itself, since without this, all authority I 3 per-

pernicious, and should be considered of no importance by prudent people: Not by whom, but what is said should be attended to, and no one should be so addicted to the judgment of others as to be entirely deprived of their own.
      The true method consists in the knowledge of the Disease and its Cure, namely, that which expels the disease by means of diet and suitable medicines, and introduces health: Therefore, Wimpenaeus learnedly discusses that the most serious diseases are cured today by Paracelsians for three reasons.
      Firstly, because diseases are known more perfectly, for formerly, when all [diseases] were referred to the four humors, those could not be cured whose cause was Tartar adhering to some member, which cannot be referred to any of those four. But since we have here come upon Tartar, a more ample mention of it must be made in this convenient place.
      From the ultimate matter of food, through the Archeus of the stomach's digestion, namely, separation and the generation of separation, emerges the first Being for Life, whence the body receives its nourishment, and sustenance: It is reduced into Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt, as appears in the three principal excretory organs: Indeed, the superfluous Salt is separated through urine, the Sulphur is excreted by being secreted through the intestines, Mercury, or the liquor of Nourishment, occupies its place; if perchance anything superfluous occurs in it, it is expelled through the pores.

ADMONITORY NOTES. 135
-tar, harmful to human health: Nature accepts nothing but what is pure: The stomach, which is the instrument of the Archæus of Man, or the innate Internal Chemist implanted by God, immediately upon receiving food and ingested matter, separates the impure, dreggy, Tartareous matter from the pure Nourishment: if the stomach is strong, and especially by its separating power, the pure passes to the members for the sake of nourishment, the impure exits through excretion: if the stomach is weak, the impure is sent even through the mesenteric veins to the liver; there a second digestion and separation occurs: The liver, therefore, in turn separates the pure from the impure from those two [substances], namely Ruby from Crystal: Ruby is the nourishment of all members, of the heart, brain, etc. Crystal, or that which is not nourishment, it expels to the kidneys, and is urine, which is nothing other than Salt pressed out from Mercurial substances by the violence of separation, forced into resolution, which is resolved by the liver into Water and expelled: If the liver, due to weakness, does not separate correctly, it sends mucilaginous and calculous matter to the kidneys; there, in the absence of good separation, by the power of predestination * through the spirit of Salt, it coagulates into Sand or Tartar or Bolus or Mucilaginous matter. Tartar, therefore, is the Excrement of food and drink, which coagulates in man through the spirit of Salt, unless by its own expulsive force it is mixed with excrements and and simultaneously excreted.
